Triggers.value: People who look similar to the victims

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I detach myself from the memories

Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: The inaction/self-blame item is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. In a child victim context, 'not doing more to stop what happened' implies agency that is typically not clinically plausible for the same trauma profile; a more general shame/self-blame item would fit, but this specific omission-guilt wording is questionable.

Within the Threat node, 'difficulty concentrating' is not a threat appraisal but a general arousal/cognitive symptom. The other Threat items reflect current danger and hypervigilance ('strong physical reactions to reminders', 'need to stay alert to fall asleep'). This item weakens within-node coherence and does not match the node's formulation role as perceived current threat.

vignette: Manaia was fifty-six years old, a detective who had spent thirty years walking into rooms where other people had done terrible things. He was divorced, living alone in a small house near the coast, and he had come to therapy because he could no longer sleep without drinking himself into a stupor. What he remembered—what he could not stop remembering—was the smell of burnt kerosene and the feel of his father’s hand closing around his wrist when he was eight years old. His father had been a fisherman, a man who drank and who believed that fear made boys strong. The abuse had not been constant, but it had been predictable: the smell of the kerosene heater, the sound of the front door opening late, the way his father’s voice would drop into something quiet and deliberate before the first blow. Manaia had learned to read the signs. He had also learned that when he tried to explain any of this to anyone—his mother, a teacher, a social worker who visited once—the thread of the story would slip from his hands. He would stammer, lose the sequence, and end up standing in silence while the other person looked at him with pity or disbelief. He had come to believe that this proved something about him: that he was a lousy coper, that the event had happened to him because of the sort of person he was. And each time the memory surfaced unbidden—the smell of kerosene, the feel of his father's hand—he felt that belief harden into something more certain, as though the intrusion itself was proof that he could not move past it. These beliefs had settled into him the way dust settles into a room that no one cleans. They were not thoughts he examined. They were the air he breathed. The past did not stay in the past. Something in his surroundings—a flicker of light, the sound of a heavy door closing—could instantly bring back the full memory without warning, and when it did, the rage that flooded him was so dense and immediate that he had once punched a hole in his own kitchen wall. After these episodes, he started taking the long way home from the station, adding forty minutes to his drive, because the route that passed the docks—the smell of salt and diesel—was the fastest way to bring it all back. He had been standing at the stove, and the burner had clicked on, and for a moment the smell of gas had been the smell of kerosene, and then he was eight years old again and his father was in the room. After that memory broke through, he began noticing the smell of gas everywhere—in the station's break room, in a neighbor's barbecue, in the exhaust of a passing truck—each one a new thread pulling him back toward that kitchen. The memory did not arrive as a story. It arrived as a body state: heart hammering, hands shaking, a heat in his chest that demanded action. Manaia had learned to manage these moments by detaching himself from the memories, pushing them away before they could fully form. He had also learned to avoid people altogether. He had stopped going to the station bar after shifts. And each place he avoided—the bar, the docks, the street where his sister lived—became its own kind of trigger, a landmark in the geography of what he could not face. But the longer he avoided it—the longer he refused to speak about the memory or let himself feel it fully—the more it seemed to press against the edges of his awareness, waiting for the moment his guard dropped. He had stopped answering calls from his sister. He had stopped wearing button-down shirts because the fabric reminded him of the shirt his father had worn the night he broke Manaia’s collarbone. The avoidance worked, for a while. But it had a cost. His captain had noticed his absences. His colleagues had stopped inviting him to case reviews. He had become the detective who worked alone, the one who took the cold cases nobody else wanted because they required no collaboration, no small talk, no risk of someone touching his shoulder from behind. The hypervigilance was constant. He could not fall asleep without checking the locks three times, without positioning himself so that he could see the bedroom door. Living at that pitch of alertness, he found that the ordinary sounds of his own house—the creak of a floorboard, the hum of the refrigerator—had become signals he could not ignore, each one demanding his full attention. This unrelenting sense of danger had quietly convinced him that his life was permanently reduced—that he was no longer the person who could sit with his back to a room or walk through a doorway without scanning for exits. He had difficulty falling asleep because he needed to stay alert, and when he did sleep, he woke at the smallest sound—a floorboard creaking, the refrigerator kicking on—and his heart would be pounding before he knew why. He had come to believe that the world was not safe, that it had never been safe, and that his reactions since the event—the rage, the avoidance, the sleeplessness—only confirmed what he already knew: that he was not the kind of person who could handle things. This belief looped back on itself. The more he avoided people, the more isolated he became, and the more isolated he became, the more convinced he was that he was fundamentally broken. He had tried, once, to tell a therapist about the abuse. He had sat in the chair, opened his mouth, and lost the thread entirely. He had left after fifteen minutes and never gone back. What finally brought him in was a case. A missing boy, twelve years old, from a family that lived near the docks. The boy’s father was a fisherman. Manaia had walked into the house and smelled kerosene, and for a moment he had been unable to move. The memory had hit him without warning: his father’s hand, the smell, the cold linoleum floor. After three years of this—of pushing it down, of turning away from his sister's calls, of refusing to let the memory take shape—he had started to believe that he was a weaker man than his father had ever been, because his father had never needed to run from his own past. He had excused himself, gone to the bathroom, and stood with his hands gripping the sink while the rage built and then subsided. He had finished the interview. He had found the boy three days later, alive, hiding in a friend’s shed. But the experience had shaken something loose. He had gone home that night and sat in the dark, and he had understood, for the first time, that he could not keep doing this alone. He was afraid of what he might do the next time the rage came. He was afraid of what he had already become.

violations.explanation: Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies: No paragraph conveys that triggers (e.g., flicker of light, sound of a door) directly cause or lead to maladaptive strategies (avoidance, detachment); triggers bring back memory, but the strategies are described as separate responses.

Memory → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that the memory itself directly causes or leads to negative appraisals; the negative beliefs are described as longstanding and not explicitly caused by the memory.
Memory → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that the memory causes or leads to triggers; triggers are described as external stimuli that evoke the memory, not the reverse.
Threat → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that the sense of threat causes or leads to negative appraisals; the threat is described as constant, but the causal link to appraisals is absent.
Threat → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that the sense of threat causes or leads to triggers; triggers are described as external cues, not as a result of threat.
Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies (avoidance, detachment) cause or lead to the memory; the strategies are used to manage the memory, not to produce it.

Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies cause or lead to negative appraisals; the appraisals are described as pre-existing or reinforced by isolation, not by the strategies themselves.
Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies cause or lead to triggers; triggers are described as external stimuli independent of the strategies.

  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies cause or lead to triggers; triggers are described as external stimuli independent of the strategies.

  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
